name: Uma Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Uma, and thank you for this. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential, so feel free to separate what you'd say out loud from what you actually think. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a transmission crew for the regional grid company, so the big steel towers, not the poles on your street. Most weeks we're out Monday to Thursday, staying in a motel near whatever line we're on, up at five, on the tower by seven. A lot of it is replacing insulators and hardware on lines that have been switched off for us, sixty metres up. On a clear morning you can see three towns from up there, and I never get tired of that.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Being away. My partner Tomas teaches at a primary school, so he's home every night and I'm in a motel in Millbrook eating noodles out of a cup. It's also still mostly men, there are two of us women on the whole transmission side. The money makes up for a lot, though. We own our flat and I've got about eight months of savings on top.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, good, can we talk about something that matters now, like pensions or the motel allowance. I'm not the type to post about it. Maybe a joke in the crew group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd mean my life stays as it is, which mostly suits me. The tower doesn't care how clever the computer in the office is. I'd keep climbing until I decided I'd had enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Keep putting money aside, keep the flat, maybe start talking seriously with Tomas about kids in a year or two. Nothing about this picture would change my plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly relieved, if I'm honest, because you hear so much about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use AI for anything now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. The tower manufacturer's manuals come in a mess of languages, and I'll ask it to translate a page. I also used it once to tidy up an incident report because my writing gets stiff when I'm tired. I check everything it gives me, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes, is there anything about the job you'd want changed anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer nights away. That's a union fight, not a technology one. If AI did nothing but sort the rosters fairly, I'd take that.

S0.say: She'd shrug it off and steer the talk back to things that matter now, like pensions and the motel allowance. At most she'd make a joke in the crew group chat.
S0.think: She believes her life would stay as it is, which mostly suits her, because the tower doesn't care how clever the office computers are. She'd keep climbing until she chose to stop.
S0.do: Carries on with work and saving, keeps the flat and starts talking seriously with her partner about having children in a year or two. Changes nothing else.
S0.feel: Calm and slightly relieved after hearing so much hype.
S0.quote: The tower doesn't care how clever the computer in the office is.
S0.fieldNote: Uma already uses AI lightly and practically, for translations and tidying reports, and checks its work. Her real complaints are nights away and fairness on the roster, which she frames as union issues. Children are on her horizon and came up without prompting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to change how we work and we need a say in how. At the union branch I'd ask for training to be paid for, not something we do on our own time. Online I'd share stories about workers getting a fair deal, or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this one mostly helps me. Inspections, planning outages, the endless forms, a lot of that could go to software, and I'd still be the one bolting the hardware on. It might even mean fewer weeks away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to go on whatever course the company runs for the new tools, and I'd learn them properly once I saw they worked. I'd also push at branch meetings for a written agreement that new tools don't mean smaller crews. That's about it, I wouldn't change jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. Curious, actually. A bit wary of management, but that's normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you seen anything at work that makes this picture feel real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At a trade fair last spring I watched a robot that crawls along a live line and checks it for damage. It was slow and clumsy, but it worked. That's the kind of thing I'd expect in this picture, and it'd do the boring part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would struggle most with this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Arno, our foreman. He's brilliant on a tower but he hates screens, he prints his emails. If the job turns into tablets and dashboards, he'd suffer. I'd want the company to give people like him time.

S1.say: She'd say the change is coming and workers need a say in how. At the union branch she'd push for paid training rather than training on her own time.
S1.think: She thinks this picture mostly helps her: software takes inspections, outage planning and forms, while she still bolts on the hardware. It might even cut her weeks away.
S1.do: Signs up for company courses on new tools and learns them properly once they prove themselves. Pushes at branch meetings for a written agreement that new tools don't mean smaller crews.
S1.feel: Calm and curious, with the usual wariness of management.
S1.quote: It was slow and clumsy, but it worked.
S1.fieldNote: She has actually seen a line-crawling inspection robot, which gives her views weight and makes her less dismissive than she might otherwise be. She expects it to take the dull work rather than her job. Her concern is for older colleagues like her foreman who struggle with screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we have unions and why the government has to act now, not after. Robots on towers would save the company a fortune, and that money needs to go somewhere other than the shareholders. I'd post about that, which I never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, that robot at the trade fair goes from clumsy to good in two years and I'm out. I'm twenty-seven, I've got maybe forty years of working life left, and I don't know what I'd do with it. The flat and the savings mean I wouldn't be on the street, but that's not the same as having a life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put more away straight away, probably the money we'd set aside for a holiday in the spring. I'd go to the branch and ask what our plan is, and I'd join whatever campaign there is for public support for people pushed out. I'd write to my representative, which I've never done in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, we'd be all right for money, but anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned kids earlier. Does this change that conversation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I think we'd put it off. You don't want to start a family the same year you find out your trade is gone. Tomas would say we'd manage, and maybe he's right, but I'd want to see where we land first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, what can you actually prepare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, honestly. Two years isn't enough to retrain for something solid, and anyway what would I retrain for, if it does everything. So it's money and pressure on politicians. That's all you can do in two years.

S2.say: She'd say this is exactly why unions exist and why government must act now, with the savings from robots going to more than shareholders. She'd post about it, which she never does.
S2.think: She believes that if the robot she saw goes from clumsy to good in two years, she's out, with forty working years left and no idea what to do. The flat and savings keep her safe from hardship but not from losing her sense of purpose.
S2.do: Moves the spring holiday money into savings, asks her union branch for its plan and joins any campaign for public support for displaced workers. Writes to her representative for the first time and puts off starting a family.
S2.feel: Anxious but not panicking, because money isn't the immediate problem.
S2.quote: You don't want to start a family the same year you find out your trade is gone.
S2.fieldNote: The most concrete effect of a two-year warning was on her plans for children, not her finances. She separates financial safety from having a life, which seemed important to her. She sees no point retraining in this picture and puts everything into collective and political pressure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much what I said before, but I'd be more organised about it. I'd say the government has five years to set up proper support and retraining, and if they waste it, that's on them. I'd be telling the younger ones on the crew to join the union if they haven't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is enough to get somewhere else in the industry before the wave hits. Not safe forever, but further back in the queue. And I'd be thirty-two, still young enough to start over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the grid control room trainee programme, where you watch the whole network and switch things remotely. It's a two-year course and the company pays. I'd keep saving and stay active at the branch while I did it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd feel like I was doing something, which helps a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the first two or three years of warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once I'd seen it coming for real, I'd actually start, because it'd be proven by then. I don't jump on things the first week, but I don't sit still when the evidence is there either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Like you said with the fast one, would kids be on hold again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not on hold. Maybe a year later than we'd planned. With five years and a plan, I think Tomas and I would go ahead.

S3.say: She'd say government has five years to set up proper support and retraining, and wasting it is on them. She'd urge younger crew members to join the union.
S3.think: She thinks five years is enough to move elsewhere in the industry before the wave arrives, not safe forever but further back in the queue. At thirty-two she'd still feel young enough to start over.
S3.do: Applies for the company-paid, two-year grid control room trainee programme, once the change is proven. Keeps saving and stays active at her union branch.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but steadier for having a plan she's working on.
S3.quote: Not safe forever, but further back in the queue.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns her from protest to planning: she names a specific company course and its length. Her steady nature shows in waiting for proof before acting, then acting firmly. The children question softens from putting it off to a one-year delay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to do this fairly, so there's no excuse for doing it badly. I'd keep making that point at the branch and in the group chat. I'd be less angry about it, more stubborn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, a decade feels manageable for me. I'd be thirty-seven, probably well into a control room job, maybe with a child. The end point still worries me, because if it really does everything, the control room goes too, eventually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the control room course, but without rushing, maybe in three or four years once I'd seen how fast it's moving. I'd vote and campaign for a proper public fund for people whose jobs go. Day to day, I'd keep climbing and enjoying it while it lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy in the background, but mostly fine. It's far enough away to plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does a decade feel like enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Enough for me. Not for Arno, he'd be close to retirement by then, but it would land badly for the forty-five-year-olds. I'd worry for them more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the government in those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A fund paid for by the companies using the robots, and free retraining that pays you while you do it. If they can make robots climb towers, they can manage that.

S4.say: She'd say a decade is plenty of time to do this fairly, so doing it badly would be inexcusable. She'd keep making that point at the branch, less angry and more stubborn.
S4.think: She feels a decade is manageable: at thirty-seven she'd likely be in a control room job and maybe a mother. The end point still worries her because the control room would eventually go too.
S4.do: Plans to take the control room course in three or four years, once she's seen the pace, and keeps climbing until then. Votes and campaigns for a public fund for people whose jobs disappear.
S4.feel: A background unease, but mostly fine because there's time to plan.
S4.quote: Not for Arno, he'd be close to retirement by then, but it would land badly for the forty-five-year-olds.
S4.fieldNote: Uma is clear that a decade works for her personally, and her concern shifts to middle-aged colleagues. She is honest that even the control room is only a temporary refuge. Her politics stay consistent across the speeds: companies using robots should pay for retraining and support.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it's the only one where I couldn't do anything for myself except wait and protest. What would help is training that pays you while you do it, and some kind of public fund that's ready before it happens, not set up after.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what it's like for women in trades. It took me years to be taken seriously on the towers. If the jobs shrink, I'm worried the first to go are the people who were last to get in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Thank you. That's everything I needed.

headlineQuote: If the jobs shrink, I'm worried the first to go are the people who were last to get in.
portrait: Uma Varga is a 27-year-old transmission lineworker on a regional grid company's tower crew, one of two women on that side of the business. She owns a flat with her partner Tomas, a primary school teacher, has about eight months saved and uses AI now and then for translations and reports. She stays calm through the milder pictures, having seen a clumsy line-inspection robot that she expects to take the dull work. A two-year AGI warning makes her anxious and puts plans for children on hold, while five or ten years turn her toward the company's grid control room programme. Throughout, she pushes for union agreements and a public fund paid for by companies using robots.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she could only wait and protest rather than act for herself.
whatWouldHelp: Paid retraining and a public fund for displaced workers set up before the change arrives rather than after.
